## Simulation study 

The simulation study by @Boulesteix_Binder_Abrahamowicz_Sauerbrei_for the Simulation Panel of the STRATOS Initiative_2018 will be reproduced in this document. It is a small scale simulation study to investigate impact of measurement error on (continuous) exposure and/or (continuous) confounding variable. 

## Data preparation

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# loading libraries
library(Hmisc)
library(mice)
library(tidyverse)
```

```{r}
# creating dataframes
d1 <- sasxport.get("data/DEMO_I.xpt")
d2 <- sasxport.get("data/BPX_I.xpt")
d3 <- sasxport.get("data/BMX_I.xpt")
d4 <- sasxport.get("data/GHB_I.xpt")
d5 <- sasxport.get("data/TCHOL_I.xpt")

d1.t <- subset(d1,select=c("seqn","riagendr","ridageyr"))
d2.t <- subset(d2,select=c("seqn","bpxsy1"))
d3.t <- subset(d3,select=c("seqn","bmxbmi"))
d4.t <- subset(d4,select=c("seqn","lbxgh"))
d5.t <- subset(d5,select=c("seqn","lbdtcsi"))

d <- merge(d1.t,d2.t)
d <- merge(d,d3.t)
d <- merge(d,d4.t)
d <- merge(d,d5.t)
```

```{r}
# rename variables:
# RIAGENDR - Gender
# RIDAGEYR - Age in years at screening
# BPXSY1 - Systolic: Blood pres (1st rdg) mm Hg
# BMXBMI - Body Mass Index (kg/m**2)
# LBDTCSI - Total Cholesterol (mmol/L)
# LBXGH - Glycohemoglobin (%)

d$age <- d$ridageyr
d$sex <- d$riagendr
d$bp <- d$bpxsy1
d$bmi <- d$bmxbmi
d$HbA1C <- d$lbxgh
d$chol <- d$lbdtcsi
d$age[d$age<18] <- NA
```

```{r}
# select complete cases:
dc <- cc(subset(d,select=c("age","sex","bmi","HbA1C","bp")))
# analysis:
summary(lm(bp ~ HbA1C + age + as.factor(sex), data=dc))
confint(lm(bp ~ HbA1C + age + as.factor(sex), data=dc))
summary(lm(bp ~ HbA1C + bmi + age + as.factor(sex), data=dc))
confint(lm(bp ~ HbA1C + bmi + age + as.factor(sex), data=dc))
```

## The Simulation

The code did not have any comments and did not specify a numeric seed. I have added this to make it more reproducible. As mentioned above, the simulation investigates the impact of measurement error on a continuous exposure and/or a continuous confounding variable. In this case, the continuous exposure is the variable HbA1C and the potential continuous confounding variables are bmi and age. Sex is also added as a control variable. The outcome variable is bp (bloodpressure). First, a linear regression is fit to get reference (ref) coefficients. Measurement error is added by adding normally distributed random errors (rnorm) to only the variables HbA1C and bmi. The simulation works with scenarios, which represent levels of error, from 0% to 50% of total variance. Regression models are fit for these scenario's.


```{r}
# setting a seed to make the simulation reproducible
set.seed(41126)

# specifying linear regression model with original data
# the coefficient for HbA1C is taken with $coef[2]
ref <- lm(bp ~ HbA1C + bmi + age + as.factor(sex), data=dc)$coef[2]

# define how many times the simulation is repeated
n.sim <- 1e3

# measurement error variance percentages
perc.me.exp <- seq(0,.5,.1)
perc.me.conf<- seq(0,.5,.1)

# combining measurement error scenarios
scenarios <- expand.grid(perc.me.exp,perc.me.conf)

# variance calculations
var.exp <- var(dc$HbA1C)
var.conf <- var(dc$bmi)

# sample size
n <- dim(dc)[1]

# creating storage object for estimated coefficients
beta.hat <- matrix(ncol=dim(scenarios)[1], nrow=n.sim)

# creating storage object for upper and lower bound confidence interval
ci_lower <- matrix(ncol=dim(scenarios)[1], nrow=n.sim)
ci_upper <- matrix(ncol=dim(scenarios)[1], nrow=n.sim)

# creating for loop which performs the simulation 1000 times
for (k in 1:n.sim){
  
# for loop which goes through all measurement error scenario's
for (i in 1:dim(scenarios)[1]){
  
  # measurement error variance divided by scenarios for coefficients
    var.me.exp <- var.exp*scenarios[i,1]/(1-scenarios[i,1])
    var.me.conf <- var.conf*scenarios[i,2]/(1-scenarios[i,2])
    
  # simulating normally distributed measurement error to both coefficients
    dc$HbA1C.me <- dc$HbA1C + rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(var.me.exp) )
    dc$bmi.me <- dc$bmi + rnorm(n, 0, sqrt(var.me.conf) )
    
  # fitting linear regression again
    beta.hat[k,i] <- lm(bp ~ HbA1C.me + age + bmi.me + as.factor(sex),
                        data=dc)$coef[2]
    
  # creating confidence interval around continuous exposure variable
    confidence_interval<- confint(lm(bp ~ HbA1C.me + age + bmi.me +  as.factor(sex), data=dc), "HbA1C.me")
    
    ci_lower[k,i]<- confidence_interval[1,1]
    ci_upper[k,i]<- confidence_interval[1,2]
   }
  }
```


## Visualising results

```{r}

# first calculating the regression coefficient across simulation for all scenarios
tot.mat <- cbind(100*scenarios, apply(beta.hat,2,mean))

# naming the column in the created matrix
colnames(tot.mat) <- c("me.exp","me.conf","estimate")

# creating figure to display the estimated regression coefficients
FIGURE <- ggplot(tot.mat, aes(me.exp, me.conf)) +
  
# figure design choices
  geom_tile(color="white",aes(fill = estimate)) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(estimate, 2))) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low="#D55E00",mid="white",high = "#56B4E9", midpoint=ref) +
  
# labeling axes
  labs(x=paste("% of total variance of HbA1c due to measurement error"),
       y=paste("% of total variance of BMI due to measurement error")) +
  coord_equal()+
  scale_y_continuous(breaks=unique(tot.mat[,1]))+
  scale_x_continuous(breaks=unique(tot.mat[,1]))+

# more customization
  theme(panel.background = element_rect(fill='white', colour='grey'),
        plot.title=element_text(hjust=0),
        axis.ticks=element_blank(),
        axis.title=element_text(size=12),
        axis.text=element_text(size=10),
        legend.title=element_text(size=12),
        legend.text=element_text(size=10))
FIGURE
# savePlot("Figure_STRATOS.tif", type="tif")
```

## Interpretation (bias, confidence intervals) and results

Before interpreting the results, we will inspect bias. The bias of an estimator is the expected value (mean) of the estimator minus the value being estimated. So we calculate the mean of betas and then subtract the reference betas.

```{r}
# first calculating the mean of all estimated coefficients using the apply function, 2 to indicate matrix columns
mean_beta<- apply(beta.hat, 2, mean)

# the bias is the difference between the mean_beta and the reference
100*(mean_beta - ref)/ref
```

For confidence interval coverage, we use also use the reference beta's

```{r}
# we want to check if a confidence interval contrains the coefficients of the reference
coverage<- ci_lower <= ref & ci_upper >= ref
coverage2<- colMeans(coverage)
coverage2
coverage3<- coverage2 >= 0.95
```

The visualization of the simulation results show that the coefficient of HbA1C decreases whenever the measurement error is increased. In addition, increasing the measurement error in bmi also increases the estimated HbA1C coefficient. Measurement error in the continuous exposure HbA1C underestimates the association with blood pressure. 

In terms of bias, a difference value of 0 means that the estimated coefficient and the reference coefficient are equal. When the difference is negative, the coefficient is underestimated in comparison with the reference and when the difference is positive, it is overestimated. We find biases around 0 when there is not measurement error. When the measurement error in HbA1C is increased, its coefficient gets underestimated, which gets stronger for even scenario with more measurement error. Overall, it is shown that measurement error in the variables biases the estimates.

As for confidence interval coverage, I assume we adhere a 95% CI. We find that this level it achieved by 21 of the scenarios. This means that 15 scenarios do not achieve a confidence interval coverage of 95%. It is noticeable that coverage decreases when measurement error on HbA1C increases.
